result: Phosphorylation of Spc110(1–220) by Mps1 and Cdk1 kinases regulates its interaction with γ-TuSC. Spc110(1–220) purified from insect cells, which harbors phosphorylations on established Mps1 and Cdk1 sites, induces an apparent shift of γ-TuSC towards the void-volume in gel filtration, whereas non-phosphorylated Spc110(1–220) from E. coli does not alter the γ-TuSC elution profile.
evaluation: Claims C34–C38 provide converging evidence from mass spectrometry (C34), gel filtration chromatography (C36, C37), and interpretation (C38) that phosphorylation of Spc110 by Mps1 and Cdk1 alters its interaction with γ-TuSC. The experimental data are internally consistent and support the conclusion.

result: Phosphomimetic mutations in Spc110(1–220) at Cdk1 sites (2D), Mps1 sites (3D), or both (5D) induce γ-TuSC oligomerization as assessed by gel filtration, whereas non-phosphorylatable mutations (5A) do not. This suggests that phosphorylated Spc110 induces oligomerization of γ-TuSC.
evaluation: Claims C39–C43 demonstrate that phosphomimetic mutations recapitulate the effect of in vivo phosphorylation on γ-TuSC oligomerization, while non-phosphorylatable mutations do not. The gel filtration data (C39–C42) and the conclusion (C43) are well-supported by the experimental evidence.

result: Electron microscopy analysis reveals that phosphomimetic Spc110(1–220) variants (2D, 3D, 5D) induce oligomeric γ-TuSC ring-like assemblies with an outer diameter of ~40 nm. The percentage of γ-TuSC spirals increases with the number of phosphomimetic mutations, suggesting that combined phosphorylation by Cdk1 and Mps1 enhances oligomerization activity.
evaluation: Claims C44–C47 provide EM evidence that phosphomimetic Spc110 induces γ-TuSC ring-like structures. The quantification (C45, C46) and interpretation (C47) are consistent with the gel filtration data and support the model that phosphorylation enhances oligomerization.

result: T18 of Spc110, identified as a phosphorylation site in prior studies, sits within a conserved motif upstream of CM1, designated as the Spc110/Pcp1 motif (SPM). Mutations at T18 (T18D, T18A, T18E, T18V) fail to induce γ-TuSC oligomerization even when combined with activating 5D mutations, suggesting that these mutations disrupt an important structural element within SPM.
evaluation: Claims C48–C53 identify the SPM motif and demonstrate that T18 mutations inactivate γ-TuSC oligomerization. The gel filtration data (C49), growth assays (C50), and sequence alignment (C52) support the conclusion that T18 is part of a functionally important motif.

result: Both the SPM and CM1 motifs of Spc110 are required for γ-TuSC oligomerization. Spc110(1–220)-5D-CM1-QA and Spc110(1–220)-5D-ΔSPM mutant proteins fail to activate γ-TuSC oligomerization even when the five activating Cdk1 and Mps1 mutations are present.
evaluation: Claims C54–C56 demonstrate that both SPM and CM1 are necessary for γ-TuSC oligomerization. The gel filtration data (C54, C55) and the conclusion (C56) are well-supported by the experimental evidence.

result: Phosphorylation of Spc110 on S36, S60, T64, T68, and S91 promotes γ-TuSC binding to Spc110. Both CM1 and SPM motifs contribute to γ-TuSC binding, as mutations in either motif reduce binding, and the double mutant shows further reduction.
evaluation: Claims C57–C61 provide GST-pulldown data demonstrating that phosphorylation and both motifs are important for γ-TuSC binding. The quantification (C57, C59, C60) and interpretation (C58, C61) are consistent and well-supported.

result: In vitro MT nucleation assays show that phosphomimetic Spc110(1–220) variants (2D, 3D, 5D) increase MT nucleation activity ~3-fold compared to buffer control and γ-TuSC alone, whereas non-phosphorylated Spc110(1–220)-WT and Spc110(1–220)-5D-T18D do not. This supports the model that Cdk1 and Mps1 phosphorylations regulate γ-TuSC-mediated MT nucleation by controlling template assembly.
evaluation: Claims C62–C65 provide in vitro MT nucleation data that are consistent with the oligomerization and binding data. The quantification (C62) and interpretation (C65) support the model that phosphorylation regulates MT nucleation.

result: Cell cycle-dependent phosphorylation of Spc110 by Cdk1 and Mps1 occurs in S phase and mitosis. Spc110S36 and Spc110S91 are phosphorylated equally by Cdk1-Clb2 and Cdk1-Clb5 in vitro. In vivo, no phosphorylation is detected in G1, but phosphorylation of Mps1 sites appears in S phase and is maintained in mitosis, while Cdk1 sites show increasing phosphorylation from S phase through mitosis.
evaluation: Claims C66–C69 and C74 provide in vitro kinase assays and in vivo immunoblot data demonstrating cell cycle-dependent phosphorylation. The data are consistent with prior reports and support the conclusion that Cdk1 and Mps1 sites are phosphorylated in S and mitosis.

result: T18 of Spc110 is phosphorylated by Cdk1-Clb2 but not Cdk1-Clb5 in vitro. In vivo, pT18 is detected in the SPB-containing pellet fraction of prometaphase cells but not in G1 or S phase arrested cells, suggesting that T18 phosphorylation occurs in M phase. In vitro phosphorylation of T18 by Cdk1-Clb2 inhibits γ-TuSC oligomerization, suggesting that T18 phosphorylation may negatively regulate SPM function.
evaluation: Claims C70–C73 and C75 provide in vitro kinase assays, mass spectrometry, and gel filtration data demonstrating that T18 is phosphorylated in M phase and that this phosphorylation inhibits γ-TuSC oligomerization. The data are consistent and support the conclusion.

result: In vivo growth assays show that spc110T18D and spc110ΔSPM cells display conditional lethal growth defects at 37°C, and the spc110T18D-CM1-QA double mutant is non-viable at 23°C and 37°C. Combining T18D with phosphomimetic mutations (2D, 3D, 5D) slightly reduces growth at 37°C, indicating that the SPM mutation T18D is dominant over the activating Cdk1 and Mps1 phosphomimetic mutations.
evaluation: Claims C76–C79 provide growth assay data demonstrating that SPM and CM1 mutations impair cell viability, and that T18D is dominant over activating mutations. The data are consistent with the in vitro oligomerization results and support the conclusion.

result: In vivo analysis of GFP-Tub1 signal at SPBs shows that SPM-defective spc110T18A and spc110T18D cells have reduced tubulin signal in G1, and all spc110 mutants except spc1105D show marked reduction in MT nucleation in S phase. The overall spindle MT signal is reduced in spc1105A, spc110T18A, spc110T18D, and spc1105D-T18D cells in metaphase. In vivo MT nucleation assays confirm that MT nucleation activity is reduced in spc1105A, spc110T18A, spc110T18D, and spc1105D-T18D cells. These data suggest that Spc110's ability to stimulate MT nucleation is regulated through stimulatory phosphorylation and requires the SPM motif.
evaluation: Claims C80–C85 provide in vivo fluorescence microscopy and MT nucleation assay data that are consistent with the in vitro data. The quantification and interpretation support the conclusion that phosphorylation and SPM are required for MT nucleation in vivo.

result: The N-terminal region of Spc98/GCP3 orthologs is conserved and contains five predicted helices followed by an unstructured linker region. N-terminal truncations of SPC98 support cell growth at 23°C but show reduced or no growth in mad2Δ cells at 37°C. spc98Δ1–156 cells have weaker GFP-Tub1 signal at SPBs at 37°C. Spc110(1–220)-5D fails to shift γ-TuSC(Spc98Δ1–156) to the void volume in gel filtration, and γ-TuSC(Spc98Δ1–156) shows reduced binding to Spc110(1–220)-5D in pulldown assays. However, γ-TuSC(Spc98Δ1–156) oligomerizes in BRB80 buffer with equal efficiency to wild-type γ-TuSC. These data suggest that the N-terminus of Spc98 is important for Spc110-mediated oligomerization but not for Spc110-independent γ-TuSC oligomerization.
evaluation: Claims C86–C95 provide sequence alignment, growth assays, fluorescence microscopy, gel filtration, and pulldown data demonstrating that the N-terminus of Spc98 is important for Spc110-mediated oligomerization. The data are internally consistent and support the conclusion.

result: Bioinformatic analysis identifies a CM1 motif in budding yeast Spc72 and predicts SPM and CM1 motifs in mammalian PCNT. Based on the presence of SPM and CM1 motifs, γ-TuCRs can be divided into SPM-CM1 (Spc110, Pcp1, PCNT) and CM1-only (Spc72, Mto1, Cnn, CDK5RAP2, myomegalin) types. γ-TuCR family proteins can be classified regarding the γ-TuSC interaction motifs and the MTOC targeting domain into three groups.
evaluation: Claims C96–C100 and C105 provide bioinformatic analysis identifying conserved motifs in γ-TuCRs. The sequence alignments and motif identification support the classification of γ-TuCRs into distinct groups.

result: Yeast Spc110, Pcp1, Drosophila D-PLP, and mammalian PCNT are targeted to the nuclear side of SPBs or centrosomal MTOCs via the conserved PACT domain. SPM-CM1 γ-TuCRs function in organizing nuclear MTs in organisms with SPBs embedded in the nuclear envelope. CM1-only γ-TuCRs of fungi have a MASC motif and function at the cytoplasmic side of the SPB or in the cytoplasm, while CM1-only γ-TuCRs of metazoa possess a CM2 domain and are targeted to both centrosomal and acentrosomal MTOCs.
evaluation: Claims C101–C104 provide bioinformatic analysis and citations to prior work demonstrating that different types of γ-TuCRs have distinct C-terminal targeting domains and functions. The data support the classification of γ-TuCRs based on their targeting domains.

result: Spc110 is a MT nucleation regulator. Binding of γ-TuSC to Spc110 is a prerequisite for γ-TuSC oligomerization into the ring-like template that initiates MT assembly. Phosphorylation of Spc110 by Cdk1 and Mps1 regulates γ-TuSC binding and thereby MT nucleation. In G1/S phase, Mps1 and Cdk1-Clb5 phosphorylate the N-terminus of Spc110 at five sites to promote γ-TuSC binding to Spc110. Mps1 and Cdk1-Clb5 coordinate the timing of MT nucleation through Spc110 phosphorylation with SPB duplication.
evaluation: Claims C106–C108, C111, and C112 provide a model for how Spc110 regulates MT nucleation through phosphorylation-dependent γ-TuSC binding and oligomerization. The model is well-supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

result: Cdk1-Clb2 phosphorylation of Spc110T18 may limit the MT nucleation activity of the SPB-associated γ-TuSC. This model fits with the observation that the yeast SPB of haploid cells organizes a constant number of 20 nuclear MTs during mitosis.
evaluation: Claims C113 and C114 propose a speculative model for the function of T18 phosphorylation in limiting MT nucleation. While the in vitro data (C73) support the inhibitory effect of T18 phosphorylation, the in vivo relevance and the connection to the constant number of MTs (C114) are not directly demonstrated. Further experiments are needed to validate this model.

result: Co-overexpression of SPC97, SPC98, and TUB4 does not induce MT nucleation despite γ-TuSC assembly. This suggests that γ-TuSC binding to Spc110 and γ-TuSC oligomerization are mechanistically distinct steps.
evaluation: Claims C115 and C116 cite prior work (C115) and propose a model (C116) that is consistent with the data presented in the manuscript. The model that binding and oligomerization are distinct steps is supported by the observation that some mutants bind γ-TuSC but fail to induce oligomerization.

result: The N-terminal region of Spc98 exhibits homology to other GCP3 family members including human GCP3. The N-Spc98 fragment is not essential for viability at 23°C. The special SPB arrangement of Spc110 as hexameric units may compensate for the reduced in vitro binding of γ-TuSC(Spc98Δ1–156) to Spc110(1–220). Regions of γ-TuSC in addition to the N-terminal 177 amino acids of Spc98 have to interact with Spc110.
evaluation: Claims C117–C120 provide sequence alignment, growth assays, and interpretation suggesting that the N-terminus of Spc98 is important but not essential, and that other regions of γ-TuSC also interact with Spc110. The data support the conclusion, although the compensation mechanism (C119) is speculative.

result: The CM1 motif was first identified in fission yeast Mto1, and its function in γ-TuSC binding was confirmed for Mto1, centrosomin, and CDK5RAP2. The γ-TuCRs Pcp1 and Spc110 also contain putative CM1 motifs. Human PCNT falls into the γ-TuCR class, and analysis of the PCNT sequence identifies a potential CM1 in the N-terminus of PCNT. This is consistent with the γ-tubulin binding ability of human PCNT, which lies within the region that contains the SPM-CM1. Super-resolution analysis of human centrosomes has mapped the localization of γ-tubulin towards the N-terminus of PCNT.
evaluation: Claims C121–C127 provide citations to prior work and bioinformatic analysis identifying CM1 motifs in various γ-TuCRs. The data support the conclusion that CM1 is a conserved motif in γ-TuCRs, and the identification of CM1 in PCNT is consistent with prior functional studies.

result: The SPM is important for Spc110 binding to γ-TuSC and induced oligomerization of γ-TuSC. SPM co-operates with CM1 to form a bipartite binding element for the γ-TuSC. The distance between SPM and CM1 is around 90–100 amino acids in the Spc110 and Pcp1 type of receptors, and around 70 amino acids in the mammalian PCNT subfamily.
evaluation: Claims C128–C131 provide a model for how SPM and CM1 cooperate to bind γ-TuSC. The model is supported by the binding and oligomerization data, and the sequence analysis provides additional context for the conservation of these motifs.

result: In budding and fission yeast, the CM1-MASC types of γ-TuCRs (Spc72 and Mto1) have specific functions in cytoplasmic MT organization, while Spc110 and Pcp1 (SPM-CM1-PACT) organize only nuclear MTs. Human CDK5RAP2, myomegalin (CM1–CM2 types), and pericentrin (SPM-CM1-PACT type) are associated with the centrosome. However, CDK5RAP2 and myomegalin also have functions in acentrosomal MT nucleation.
evaluation: Claims C132–C135 provide citations to prior work demonstrating the functional specialization of different types of γ-TuCRs. The data support the conclusion that γ-TuCRs have distinct functions based on their motif composition and targeting domains.

result: Budding yeast organizes MTs only with γ-TuSC and γ-TuCRs. GCP4 to 6 are not essential for MT nucleation in fission yeast and Drosophila, while GCP2/Alp4, GCP3/Alp6, and Mozart1 are essential for viability. Fission yeast Mozart1 is essential for γ-TuSC recruitment to SPBs. Considering the conservation between the SPM and CM1 binding elements of γ-TuRCs and the N-terminal region of Spc98/GCP3, the basic principles of MT nucleation are conserved from yeast to human.
evaluation: Claims C136–C140 provide citations to prior work and propose a model for the conservation of MT nucleation mechanisms. The model is supported by the data presented in the manuscript and is consistent with prior studies.

result: Budding yeast Spc110 is a member of the γ-tubulin complex receptor family (γ-TuCR) and recruits γ-tubulin complexes to microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs). Biochemical studies suggest that Spc110 facilitates higher-order γ-tubulin complex assembly.
evaluation: Claims C1–C3 provide background knowledge and citations to prior work characterizing Spc110. These claims are well-established in the literature and provide context for the current study.

result: The study shows that Spc110 phosphorylated by Mps1 and Cdk1 activates γ-TuSC oligomerization and MT nucleation in a cell cycle dependent manner. Interaction between the N-terminus of the γ-TuSC subunit Spc98 and Spc110 is important for this activity. Besides the conserved CM1 motif, a second motif named Spc110/Pcp1 motif (SPM) is also important for MT nucleation. The activating Mps1 and Cdk1 sites lie between SPM and CM1 motifs. Most organisms have both SPM-CM1 and CM1-only types of γ-TuCRs, which contain distinct but conserved C-terminal MTOC targeting domains.
evaluation: Claims C4–C10 summarize the major findings of the study as stated in the abstract. These claims are supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript and represent the core contributions of the work.

result: Background knowledge on budding yeast spindle assembly, γ-TuSC structure and function, γ-TuRC assembly, Mozart1, γ-TuCRs, and Spc110 phosphorylation. These claims provide context for the current study and are supported by citations to prior work.
evaluation: Claims C11–C33 provide background knowledge and citations to prior work. These claims are well-established in the literature and provide context for the current study.
